summary: ECN lets routers mark packets instead of dropping them to signal congestion. The original TCP feedback could report only one mark per round trip. This RFC defines Accurate ECN feedback, which lets a receiver tell the sender about the number of marks, giving the sender a more detailed picture of congestion.

eli5.summary: Instead of a friend only saying "there was a traffic jam," they tell you how many red lights they hit. You can then choose your speed more wisely.

questions: how does tcp report congestion marks accurately

subtitle: A way for TCP receivers to tell senders how many packets were congestion-marked, not just whether any were.

tldr.problem: Classic ECN feedback in TCP can report only one congestion signal per round-trip time, which is not enough for mechanisms such as DCTCP and L4S that need to know about every mark.
tldr.mechanism: AccECN reuses the TCP header flags (the previously reserved NS bit, now AE, plus CWR and ECE) as a 3-bit counter of CE-marked packets, and optionally adds two TCP options with byte counters.
tldr.outcome: A sender learns how many marks arrived, can detect middlebox interference, and falls back to Classic ECN or no ECN with older peers. RFC 9768 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 3168.

today: RFC 9768 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3168; the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets network nodes mark IP packets instead of dropping them to signal incipient congestion. The receiver feeds that information back to the sender. In RFC 3168, ECN was specified for TCP in a way that allows only one feedback signal per Round-Trip Time (RTT). That is enough for Reno and CUBIC, which reduce their window by a fixed factor however many marks arrive in an RTT. It is not enough for newer mechanisms such as ConEx, DCTCP and L4S, which need to know when more than one mark arrives in an RTT.

This document defines more Accurate ECN feedback (AccECN) for TCP and updates RFC 3168 with respect to negotiation and use of the TCP feedback scheme. The IP-layer definition of ECN is unaffected. AccECN is a complete replacement for Classic ECN feedback rather than a fork, and it is solely a change to the TCP wire protocol; how a sender responds to congestion is out of scope.

The design has two parts: an essential feedback part that reuses the TCP-ECN header bits to count CE-marked packets, and a supplementary part with two new TCP options that count payload bytes per ECN codepoint. The two-part split was needed because option space is scarce and some badly designed middleboxes might block new options.
sections.eli5: The old way only said "somewhere on the road there was a jam." The new way counts the jams, so the driver knows how bad the road is.

sections.title: How Classic ECN Feedback Works
sections.content:
ECN has two halves. In the forward direction the IP header carries a 2-bit field: 0b00 is Not-ECT, 0b01 is ECT(1), 0b10 is ECT(0) and 0b11 is CE (Congestion Experienced). A node that is congested can mark an ECT packet as CE instead of dropping it; Not-ECT packets can only be dropped.

The return half is TCP's own. A Classic ECN client sets (CWR,ECE) = (1,1) on the SYN and an ECN-enabled server answers with (0,1). After a CE mark arrives, the receiver sets ECE on every ACK until the sender answers with CWR. That always produces a full RTT of ACKs with ECE set, so extra CE marks within that RTT cannot be reported.

The last bit of byte 13 of the TCP header had been defined as the Nonce Sum (NS) for the ECN-nonce of RFC 3540. Because of limited deployment RFC 3540 was reclassified as Historic by RFC 8311, and the bit returned to Reserved. AccECN reuses it.

Because AccECN reflects whatever markings it sees, it is a generic reflector: senders can adopt new behaviours later without receivers having to upgrade, and it also feeds back the IP-ECN field of the SYN and SYN/ACK, which lets endpoints detect middleboxes that overwrite the field as if it were the old Type of Service field.
sections.eli5: Classic ECN is a friend who waves a flag once per trip when the road was busy. AccECN is a friend who keeps a tally of every busy spot.

sections.title: Negotiating AccECN in the Handshake
sections.content:
The renamed AE (Accurate ECN) flag, together with CWR and ECE, is used in the three-way handshake. A client that wants AccECN MUST set (AE,CWR,ECE) = (1,1,1) on the SYN. An AccECN-enabled server that receives it MUST enter AccECN mode and set the three flags on the SYN/ACK to one of four combinations that feed back the IP-ECN field of the SYN: (0,1,0) for Not-ECT, (0,1,1) for ECT(1), (1,0,0) for ECT(0) and (1,1,0) for CE. The client MUST NOT enter AccECN mode before it has received the SYN/ACK.

The flags were chosen so that negotiation falls back naturally. A server that only knows Classic ECN reads the SYN as a request for Classic ECN and answers (0,0,1); one without ECN answers (0,0,0). An AccECN server that receives a Classic ECN SYN of (0,1,1) answers (0,0,1) and follows RFC 3168, or can answer (0,0,0) and disable ECN. Older servers that wrongly reflect the SYN flags back as (1,1,1) are 'broken', and the client MUST fall back to Not ECN mode. The combination (1,0,1) is reserved for future use.

If the SYN is lost, the client SHOULD retry AccECN once and then, where path traversal might be a problem, send later SYNs with the flags cleared, using the same initial sequence number. A host MUST NOT switch to a different feedback mode from the one it first entered, and MUST reset the connection if it sees both Classic and AccECN handshake packets in the same handshake. Once in AccECN mode, a host MUST NOT set CWR to indicate a congestion response, and MUST feed back the IP-ECN field of incoming packets.
sections.eli5: The first message is a secret handshake. If the other side knows the new handshake, you both use it. If not, you quietly use the older one.

sections.title: The ACE Field
sections.content:
After AccECN is negotiated, on any segment with SYN=0 the three flags (AE,CWR,ECE) are read together as a 3-bit ACE field. The Data Receiver keeps four counters: r.cep counts packets that arrived marked CE (including CE-marked control packets and retransmissions, but not CE on SYN packets), and r.ceb, r.e0b and r.e1b count payload bytes marked CE, ECT(0) and ECT(1). The Data Sender keeps matching s. counters. The initial values are r.cep = 5, r.e0b = r.e1b = 1 and r.ceb = 0. Non-zero values support a stateless handshake and are distinct from a field wrongly zeroed by a middlebox.

Every ACK carries the 3 least significant bits of r.cep in the ACE field. The sender subtracts the low 3 bits of its own s.cep to find the minimum positive increment, assuming the field wrapped at most once. Because 3 bits wrap quickly, the receiver follows safety rules: it SHOULD send an ACK when a CE-marked data packet follows a non-CE packet (a change-triggered ACK), and it MUST send an ACK once n CE marks have arrived since the previous ACK, where n SHOULD be 2 with unacknowledged data, SHOULD be 3 and MUST be at least 3 without it, and MUST be no more than 7. The sender, lacking the AccECN option, uses the jump in the acknowledgement number to judge whether the field cycled, taking the safest likely case.

There is one exception to the counter meaning. On the pure ACK of the SYN/ACK (no data, no SACK blocks), a client uses a handshake encoding of the ACE field to feed back the IP-ECN field of the SYN/ACK: 0b010 for Not-ECT, 0b011 for ECT(1), 0b100 for ECT(0) and 0b110 for CE. A client with data to send SHOULD first send such a pure ACK.
sections.eli5: Each reply carries a small tally from 0 to 7 that starts over after 7. The sender keeps its own tally, compares, and works out how many red lights were missed.

sections.title: The AccECN TCP Options
sections.content:
Two alternative options carry the byte counters. Both have three 24-bit fields, each holding the 24 least significant bits of a counter: Kind 172 (AccECN0, order 0) has EE0B, ECEB, EE1B; Kind 174 (AccECN1, order 1) has them in the opposite order. The receiver picks whichever order is more efficient. There is no field for Not-ECT bytes; the appendices give a way to calculate them.

To save option space, unchanged fields can be omitted from the tail, indicated by the length: 11 for all three fields, 8 for two, 5 for one and 2 for an empty option. Senders MUST be able to read all four lengths and, for forward compatibility, use whole 3-octet fields that fit within any other length. A client MUST NOT put an AccECN option on a SYN. A server SHOULD include one on the SYN/ACK, and a client SHOULD include one on the first ACK and on its first data segment, to test whether the path passes them.

On when to include the option, the recommended simple scheme is that the receiver SHOULD include it on every scheduled ACK if any byte counter has increased since the last ACK, with a field for every counter that has changed during the connection. If SACK is negotiated and the option would leave too little room for two SACK blocks, SACK takes precedence. Implementing options is optional but sending them is RECOMMENDED, since the options protect against ACK filtering that could make the 3-bit counter ambiguous.
sections.eli5: The options are a bigger scoreboard with room for larger numbers. If there is no space, the sender can leave off the parts that did not change.

sections.title: Detecting Mangling and Blocked Options
sections.content:
A big theme is that the Internet contains devices that interfere with ECN. The client can compare the IP-ECN value reported on the SYN/ACK with what it sent on the SYN, and the server can compare the ACE value on the last handshake ACK with what it sent on the SYN/ACK. An invalid transition (Not-ECT changes, ECT becomes Not-ECT, or CE changes) makes the host advised to send non-ECN-capable packets for the rest of the half-connection, but it MUST stay in AccECN mode, MUST keep feeding back marks, and ought still to respond to CE feedback. This is non-normative advice because the best strategy depends on deployment experience; asymmetric mangling is described as currently common over some mobile networks.

If a server's SYN/ACK goes unanswered it SHOULD retransmit it without the AccECN option, and then with (AE,CWR,ECE) = (0,0,0), while staying in AccECN mode. A client that sees no AccECN option on the SYN/ACK assumes options are unavailable for that half-connection and MUST use the conservative reading of the ACE field. Hosts MAY check that the initial EE0B and EE1B values are non-zero, but MUST NOT test them for specific values. Finally, if the byte counter ceb increases but the packet counter cep does not, and there is no other explanation, the Data Sender MUST stop sending ECN-capable packets for the rest of that half-connection.
sections.eli5: Some roads have bad signs that scramble messages. AccECN checks at the start that the messages came through unchanged, and plays it safe if not.

sections.title: Middleboxes, Offload and Compatibility
sections.content:
Because AccECN changes the TCP wire protocol, the RFC sets rules for equipment on the path. A TCP proxy that splits connections is compliant if each side negotiates AccECN independently. A transparent middlebox ought to forward AccECN options unaltered, whatever their length or initial values, because blocking apparently invalid values stops future extensions; and any middlebox MUST NOT change the ACE field or the currently specified AccECN option fields.

For TCP Segmentation Offload, hardware that masks out the CWR bit on middle and last segments would change the ACE field, so drivers may need minor changes. For Large Receive Offload, hardware that ejects a segment whenever the ECN flags change may cause many interrupts; the ACE counter is designed so coalescing needs to stop only when the counter wraps.

AccECN is compatible with the MSS, timestamp, window scale, SACK and TCP-AO options, with MPTCP and TCP Fast Open, and with the ECN++ experiment, and it consumes no extra header space on the SYN. A server using SYN cookies can infer AccECN from an ACE value of 0b010 to 0b111 on the ACK; 0b000 or 0b001 shows the client did not request AccECN. Three approaches can protect feedback integrity: sender tests, ConEx audit and TCP-AO.
sections.eli5: Special machines along the road must pass the tallies along without changing them. Speed-up hardware inside computers may need small tweaks so it does not smudge the numbers.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
If the AccECN options are unusable, the 3-bit ACE field offers only limited resilience to long runs of ACK loss. The RFC considers this safe because without options the sender must assume more conservative wrapping. Such problems are unlikely to be malicious, since an attacker able to strip a TCP option or drop a long run of ACKs could do other arbitrary harm.

A misbehaving receiver could suppress or alter ECN feedback to gain throughput at others' expense, which is why compatibility with the three integrity approaches matters. Allowing odd option lengths opens a potential covert channel of up to 29 bytes, which the RFC describes as overt rather than hidden and no different from unknown TCP options in general; regular TCP normalizers can close it. AccECN is not believed to add new privacy concerns, since it counts signals already visible at the IP layer. While few hosts use it, those hosts could be easier to identify.

For IANA, the RFC reassigns TCP header flag bit 7 from NS to AE (Accurate ECN) and registers option kinds 172 and 174. Earlier experimental implementations used option 254 with magic numbers 0xACC0, 0xACC1 and 0xACCE, and SHOULD migrate to the new kinds.
sections.eli5: A cheater could pretend the road was clear to go faster, so there are ways to check. The tally does not give away secrets because the road signs were already public.
